beats.t: Fried sugar greeted them as they stepped off the leaf boat. Since the black feather landed, the highest stage had stayed silent. Below, singing shops and clattering plates grew louder as though filling its absence. Hunger was the simplest proof of being alive.
They're frying clouds! Real clouds, and they don't melt.
Yeongnyangi, skip the explanation. Just tell me if I can eat them.
You can. But see what they take as payment.

A child beat a little drum in the alley, carrying the island's rhythm alone since the high stage stopped. People clapped, then lost expression when he stopped. Clear shards piled before him instead of coins, each briefly reflecting someone's smiling lips.
That isn't money. Are they giving him their laughter? Shouldn't someone first ask whether they get it back?
Returning it would hardly make a business. The receiver feels good; the giver is fed. That's enough.
If you count tomorrow's costs too, you'll never buy anything.

The black tiger sat on a red rooftop awning. The ring mark on its forepaw was hidden under the cloak, but river sand still clung to the damp gold trim. Yeoni raised a hoof in greeting. Only after checking the surroundings did the tiger nod.
Is your paw okay? Come down. I can't climb up to rescue you yet.
Do you always ask about injuries first when you meet someone again?
What a tiring habit.
The tiger's red eyes moved to Yeoni's crown. New red, silver, and blue ornaments nestled among her petals. Beside them, the one that had faded by the river remained white.
Three new petals, yet that one is unchanged. Decorations don't cover a place where a price was paid.

The tiger jumped down. An empty plate happened to be beneath it, but slid aside before its paw landed. Yeongnyangi noticed. Yeoni was watching only the child's drumsticks. The child gripped them so tightly that the handles dug into small palms.
He can rest. His hands are bleeding.
Applause shouldn't have to hurt that much.

The child tried to stop, then resumed drumming. A tag hanging around their neck trembled. Small print on it said they had borrowed today's applause in advance. The line saying they could not leave the stage until it was repaid was on the back.
The child chose it. An audience on credit seemed better than a song nobody heard.
Grant people their wishes, and afterward they always treat you as the villain.
He wished for applause. Not bleeding hands.
Show only the front and call it a choice? That's the cowardly part.

The tiger slowly flattened its ears. When Yeongnyangi moved in front of Yeoni, the tiger did not retreat. Instead, it pressed the red jewel at its throat with a paw. The child's drumming broke for a beat, then accelerated.
Don't touch the necklace. Break it by force, and you tear his voice.
People who write these contracts always use the victim as a shield.
Then we'll be his audience. Real applause, not borrowed.
Yeongnyangi, if you have no rhythm, just keep step beside me.

Yeoni tried to follow the quick drumbeat and fell twice. Onlookers laughed. They got up and tapped the ground again. Only after giving up on looking skilled could they properly hear the drum. The child always struggled most just before the chorus.
Rest here. I'll play until you're ready to join in again.
Nothing says you have to do it all alone.
Two little hooves beat the ground. A dull sound to call applause. Still, the child lifted his head for the first time. Someone had entered his song and taken the empty part.
Count to three and breathe. Rest a moment if you're breathless.

Yeongnyangi's tail tapped the floor. Its slow, precise sound steadied the child's hands. One onlooker followed the same rhythm. Then two, three. The alley's sound gradually changed. Among purchased cheers, newly born applause began to mingle.
Why are you pleased when you're so badly out of time? Missed beats, cracking voices and all.
He smiled at us. Being good can wait. Today his hands need a rest.
The tiger watched the child's tag. The debt carved into its front faded stroke by stroke. She pressed a corner with her paw. The strokes kept fading.

A black droplet sprang from the tiger's paw and struck the tag. The final line binding the child blurred. At the same moment, the tiny name on the tag's edge was sucked into the droplet. The child, catching their breath after setting down the drumsticks, did not see.
You helped just then. I saw.
Fold your ears if you don't want to hear thank you.
Perhaps you saw what you wished to see. Please take the child with you today.
Leave the tag, though. I clear away the papers once the account is settled.

The child broke a fried cloud in half. One half went to Yeoni; the other was placed before the tiger. The tiger looked first at the cut edges, as though measuring which portion was larger. The child smiled again without even looking at the sizes.
There's some for you too. No fine print on the back.
You can complain if it's bad, but I didn't fry it, so I can't take responsibility.
The tiger bit into the fritter. The child smiled his thanks. She looked between his smile and Yeoni's. Something rustled inside her cloak.
Let's go. Keep checking what you've given, and even gratitude becomes a shackle.

Yeoni left the alley with the child. Yeongnyangi watched the tiger's paws to the last. When the droplet at its feet slipped behind the awning, his violet eyes narrowed. The tiger swallowed the remaining food without avoiding his gaze.
Free people once, and they never look at the second line.
I wonder when you will, dear guest.

The tiger climbed onto the awning and looked down the alley. The shopkeeper who lent applause had vanished. Only the ledger remained. A red mark was stamped inside the cover—the same shape as the marking on the tiger's forehead.

The tiger erased the child's name from the original ledger. Not destroyed it: moved it into the lining of its own cloak. One golden thread turned black. The paw closing the back cover did not tremble. The tag it would show Yeoni tomorrow was clean now.
